newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-Japan PM wants strong yen, low trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Japan PM wants strong yen, low trade surplus.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Wednesday he supported a strong euro after the launch of European economic monetary union (EMU), but he did not want to see the yen become a second class currency.

Speaking at a news conference after the annual European Union-Japan summit in The Hague, Hashimoto said Japan was very interested in EMU developments and efforts were being made to educate business and institutions on the implications of a single currency.
"We would like to see it (the euro) have a status as a major currency," he said. "We have adopted a forward looking approach to the issue."
But in response to a question on Japanese business confidence and its effects on domestic Japanese interest rates, he said he also supported a strong, influential yen.
"The yen has no wish to be relegated to a local currency," he said. "As for interest rates, you know that solely belongs for others to decide."
Hashimoto said too much emphasis was being placed on Japan's trade figures, adding that the current surplus would not increase significantly in the medium term.
"It is a temporary phenomenon," he said. "On the short term both (Japanese) imports and exports have increased and that is the trend. People tend to be preoccupied by the surplus."
Earlier, an EU source said Hashimoto had told his European counterparts that comments he made on Monday in the United States regarding U.S. Treasuries had been "misunderstood".
"There was not much discussion on the issue," the source told Reuters. "He (Hashimoto) said he had been misunderstood ... perhaps unskilled."
Hashimoto said on Monday that in the past Japan had been tempted to sell some of its Treasuries but had not done so. The Finance Ministry in Tokyo said later he had been misunderstood.
"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation ... and switch to gold," he said then.
The remarks sent shivers through global financial markets but since then Japanese officials have tried to play down the issue.
Concern has also mounted over a key Japanese business survey which showed small manufacturers far more buoyant than expected, suggesting increased Japanese exports.
A joint communique issued after the summit said efforts would be made to boost cooperation on financial market deregulation, bilateral investment and trade.

The EU and Japan have agreed to accelerate work on a treaty covering mutual recognition agreements (MRA) by which goods manufactured by one side do not need to undergo checks and certification once imported by the other.
The EU last week initialled an MRA accord with the U.S. and Canada, a deal that industry analysts said could save manufacturers billions of dollars in the future.
The EU-Japan MRA treaty will cover similar areas -- medical products, pharmaceuticals and certain electrical and telecommunications equipment.
The communique said Hashimoto also urged more investment by the EU in Japan and outlined efforts by Tokyo to attract foreign firms to Japan.
